title: IAM, Resource Hierarchy, and Separation of Duties
bodyMarkdown:
## Why the hierarchy is the first control you design

Google Cloud resources form a four-tier tree: **Organization → Folders (optional) → Projects → service resources** such as VMs and buckets. Every resource except the top has exactly one parent, and a Google Workspace or Cloud Identity account maps to exactly one organization. Per the [resource hierarchy documentation](https://cloud.google.com/resource-manager/docs/cloud-platform-resource-hierarchy), IAM roles granted on a folder are inherited by every project and folder beneath it, and allow, deny, and organization policies all inherit down the tree. The effective policy on a resource is what is set on it directly **plus** what it inherits from its ancestors.

That inheritance is why hierarchy design is a security decision, not a filing exercise:

- **Organization node:** the root. Holds the baseline organization policies, a small number of org-wide IAM bindings (security reviewers, billing viewers), and the audit-log sink.
- **Folders:** model departments, teams, or environments. Attach IAM and policy here so a new project inherits the right guardrails on day one.
- **Projects:** the unit of isolation for quota, billing, APIs, and blast radius. Separate production from non-production at the project level at minimum, and preferably at the folder level so policies can differ.

Design for the smallest tree that expresses your real policy boundaries, typically environment first, then business unit or workload, and resist mirroring the org chart one-to-one.

## The IAM model

An IAM allow policy is a set of **bindings**: a **principal** (user, group, service account, federated identity) gets a **role** (a bundle of permissions) on a **resource**, optionally with a **condition**.

| Role type | What it is | Use it when |
|---|---|---|
| **Predefined** | Google-maintained, per-service, updated as the service evolves (e.g. `roles/storage.objectViewer`) | Default choice for almost everything |
| **Custom** | You assemble supported permissions; max **300 per organization** and **300 per project**; grantable only within the org/project that owns it | Predefined roles are demonstrably too broad and you can maintain the role over time |
| **Basic** (Owner, Editor, Viewer, plus newer Reader/Writer/Admin) | Very broad, cross-service access; the legacy Owner/Editor/Viewer roles do not support IAM Conditions | Prototyping only |

The [IAM roles overview](https://cloud.google.com/iam/docs/roles-overview) is blunt: in production, do not grant basic roles unless there is no alternative. Custom roles carry an operational cost: you own the permission list when services add new permissions, so prefer predefined roles first.

### When a custom role is the right answer

Prefer predefined roles; create a custom role only when every predefined role is demonstrably broader than the job needs. The [custom roles documentation](https://cloud.google.com/iam/docs/understanding-custom-roles) sets the rules that decide the design:

- **Scope is where the role can be used.** A custom role can be granted only within the project or organization that owns it. A role defined in one project cannot be granted in the other 39; define it at the **organization** to grant it on any folder or project beneath.
- **Project-level roles cannot include permissions that apply only at the organization or folder level.**
- **Support levels:** `SUPPORTED` permissions work in custom roles, `TESTING` ones may behave unexpectedly, and `NOT_SUPPORTED` ones cannot be included.
- **You maintain it.** A custom role is not updated when Google adds permissions to the predefined role you copied from, so a new feature can fail with permission-denied until you add the permission. A disabled role stays in policies but has no effect.

| Situation | Choice |
|---|---|
| One predefined role fits | Use it |
| Predefined roles are too broad for the job | Custom role at the scope where it will be granted |
| Editor plus a deny policy to carve it down | Avoid: a deny rule lists every unwanted permission, and any permission Editor gains later is allowed |

Deny policies are a guardrail on top of least-privilege grants, not a way to shrink a broad role.

### Least privilege in practice

The [IAM security best practices](https://cloud.google.com/iam/docs/using-iam-securely) reduce to a short list:

- **Grant to groups, not individuals.** Onboarding, offboarding, and audits become group-membership changes.
- **Grant at the smallest scope that works.** Remember that a child inherits everything, so a VM-admin role at project level means every VM in the project.
- **One service account per workload**, each with only the permissions that workload needs. Do not share a "god" service account across services.
- **Avoid service account keys** if any alternative exists (impersonation, Workload Identity Federation, attached service accounts). Never commit them to source control.
- **Audit policy changes** via Cloud Audit Logs and control who can modify organization-level policy.
- Use the role recommender and Policy Simulator to right-size roles before and after changes.

## Beyond allow policies: conditions, deny, and boundaries

Allow policies alone do not express every guardrail. Google Cloud layers three more IAM mechanisms.

**[IAM Conditions](https://cloud.google.com/iam/docs/conditions-overview)** attach a CEL expression to a binding. Attributes include resource type, name, service and tags, the request time, and (for IAP) destination port and URL host or path. Constraints to remember: conditions cannot be used with the legacy Owner/Editor/Viewer roles, cannot condition `allUsers` or `allAuthenticatedUsers`, and the documentation advises keeping a single allow policy to no more than **100 conditional role bindings**. Cloud Storage buckets need **uniform bucket-level access** enabled before conditions work. Which services accept conditions is covered in the time-bound section below.

**[Deny policies](https://cloud.google.com/iam/docs/deny-overview)** are checked **before** allow policies, inherit down the hierarchy, and cannot be overridden by lower levels. A resource can hold up to **500 deny policies** and **500 deny rules** in total. Rules support exception principals and exception permissions, which is how you express "nobody except the break-glass group may delete projects" without hundreds of narrow allow grants.

**Principal Access Boundary (PAB)** policies attach to **sets of principals** rather than resources. They can only **block**, never grant, which makes them an eligibility filter: for example, stop principals from reaching resources outside your organization, or confine a set of service accounts to specific projects. Documented limits include 1,000 PAB policies per organization and 500 rules per policy.

| Mechanism | Attaches to | Can it grant access? | Typical use |
|---|---|---|---|
| Allow policy | Resource | Yes | Normal role grants |
| Deny policy | Org / folder / project | No | Hard "never" rules with exceptions |
| PAB policy | Principal set | No | Limit which resources a principal set may ever reach |
| Organization Policy | Org / folder / project | No (not IAM at all) | Constrain resource *configuration* |

## Organization Policy versus IAM

The [Organization Policy overview](https://cloud.google.com/resource-manager/docs/organization-policy/overview) puts it in one line: IAM focuses on **who** can act, Organization Policy focuses on **what** can be configured. Constraints are **boolean** (enforced or not) or **list** (allowed/denied values). Descendants inherit by default and can override on the descendant resource; the permission to administer policy (`roles/orgpolicy.policyAdmin`) is separate from owning a project, so a project Owner cannot weaken a constraint set above them.

Operational points that appear in design questions:

- **Dry-run mode** audit-logs violations without denying actions. Use it to measure blast radius before enforcement.
- New constraints are **not retroactive**; existing violating resources keep running until you remediate them.
- **Tags** allow conditional enforcement, so a constraint can apply only to resources carrying a given tag.

## Separation of duties

No single person should hold two powers that together enable fraud or an unreviewed change. Model it with disjoint groups: `deployers` (deploy permissions) and `approvers` (release or attestation permissions), with nobody in both; keep `org-policy-admins` apart from workload owners; and keep Cloud KMS key administrators apart from key users. SoD is a **preventive** control; audit logs only tell you afterwards, so use both but never rely on logs alone.

For occasional elevation, [Privileged Access Manager](https://cloud.google.com/iam/docs/pam-overview) gives just-in-time grants. An **entitlement** defines who may request, which roles are granted, whether a justification and an approval are required, and the **maximum grant duration** (specifics in the time-bound section below). After approval the roles are bound with a time-based condition and are revoked automatically. PAM works at project, folder, and organization level and its events land in Cloud Audit Logs. The principle: keep permanent roles least-privilege and elevate temporarily for specific tasks.

### Scoped read-only access, a worked example

A billing analyst must see spend across the organization but must not read application data or change resources. The [Cloud Billing access documentation](https://cloud.google.com/billing/docs/how-to/billing-access) describes `roles/billing.viewer` as read access to cost and payment information that cannot link or unlink projects or manage the billing account. Granting that on the billing account (plus an org-level viewer role so the analyst can see the hierarchy) satisfies the need; granting Viewer on every project would expose application resources, and billing admin would add management rights.

## Time-bound access: IAM Conditions versus Privileged Access Manager

Two mechanisms make access expire, and they solve different problems.

**Dated conditional binding.** Put a [condition on `request.time`](https://cloud.google.com/iam/docs/configuring-temporary-access) on an ordinary binding, for example `request.time < timestamp('2026-11-24T00:00:00Z')`. The documentation's own examples bind a Google group this way, and `getHours` and `getDayOfWeek` express recurring windows such as business hours. Limits:

- The legacy Owner, Editor and Viewer roles, `allUsers` and `allAuthenticatedUsers` remain excluded, as noted above.
- Only some services accept conditional bindings. The [documented list](https://cloud.google.com/iam/docs/resource-types-with-conditional-roles) includes Compute Engine, Cloud Storage (uniform bucket-level access required), BigQuery, Cloud Run, Cloud KMS, Secret Manager, IAP and Resource Manager; for other resource types, grant the conditional role at the project or organization instead.
- A conditional binding does not override an unconditional binding of the same role, so an old permanent grant makes the expiry meaningless.

**Privileged Access Manager entitlement.** An [entitlement](https://cloud.google.com/iam/docs/pam-create-entitlements) fixes who may request (up to 20 principals directly, or groups, where every member may request but only the requester receives access), up to 30 roles on a project, folder or organization, a grant duration from **30 minutes to 7 days**, optional justification and optional approvers. A requester can withdraw a pending request. Legacy Owner, Editor and Viewer are not supported either; translate the duties into specific roles.

| Need | Use |
|---|---|
| Known window for a whole team, no approval (audit period, contractor engagement) | Dated conditional binding on predefined roles |
| On-demand elevation with justification, an approver and a record of each grant, up to 7 days | PAM entitlement |
| Continuous access longer than 7 days | Conditional binding; one entitlement grant cannot last that long |
| Owner, Editor or Viewer | Neither: choose specific predefined or custom roles |

## Evidence of least privilege at scale

Policy Intelligence ([overview](https://cloud.google.com/policy-intelligence/docs/overview)) is a set of tools for different questions.

| Question | Tool |
|---|---|
| Who can access this resource, or what can this principal reach? | Policy Analyzer |
| Why does this principal have or lack access? | Policy Troubleshooter |
| What changes if I edit this policy? | Policy Simulator |
| Which granted roles hold permissions that were not used? | IAM recommender |
| Which service accounts have not been used in 90 days? | Service account insights |

[Policy Analyzer](https://cloud.google.com/policy-intelligence/docs/policy-analyzer-overview) analyzes allow policies across an organization, folder or project scope, inherited ones included. It does not support deny policies, Principal Access Boundary policies, Kubernetes RBAC or Cloud Storage ACLs, and its results do not account for them. It shows grants, not actual use.

The [IAM recommender](https://cloud.google.com/iam/docs/recommender-overview) compares granted permissions with those used in at most the last **90 days** and suggests revoking or replacing a role, occasionally a new project-level custom role. It never applies anything: each recommendation must be reviewed, then applied or dismissed. A pile of generated recommendations is therefore not evidence of least privilege, and the reviewed outcomes are. The 90-day window can also flag quarter-end or annual jobs as unused, so review before bulk-applying. Role recommendations can also appear as findings in Security Command Center's paid tiers; the docs name Premium and Enterprise, so confirm your tier before promising this.

## Choosing the right mechanism

When a scenario asks how to enforce a rule, work through these questions in order:

1. **Is the rule about a person's or workload's ability to call an API?** Use IAM: a predefined role on a group, at the lowest node that works.
2. **Is it about how a resource may be configured** (external IPs, locations, key creation)? Use Organization Policy at the org or folder.
3. **Must it hold even if someone later grants a broad role?** Add a deny policy, with exceptions for a break-glass group.
4. **Should a set of identities never reach resources outside a boundary?** Use a PAB policy.
5. **Is the access needed only occasionally?** Use PAM or impersonation with a condition instead of a standing grant.
6. **Is it only a time-boxed or resource-scoped grant?** Use an IAM Condition on the binding.

## Common mistakes and anti-patterns

- **Basic roles in production** (Editor "to make it work"). Replace with predefined roles and verify with the recommender.
- **Granting to individuals** and never cleaning up. Use groups.
- **Flat structure**: one giant project, or prod and dev in the same project, so IAM and policy cannot differ.
- **Policy at the leaf only.** If every project is configured by hand, the third new project will drift. Set the baseline at the org or folder.
- **Confusing IAM with Organization Policy.** Granting `roles/compute.admin` cannot enable external IPs if a constraint denies them, and an org policy cannot grant anyone anything.
- **Letting workload owners hold `orgpolicy.policyAdmin`**, which defeats the guardrail.
- **Service account keys as the default** auth mechanism.
- **Assuming a deny in a parent can be undone below.** Lower-level policies cannot override a higher deny; use exceptions in the deny rule itself.
- **A custom role created in one project and expected to work elsewhere.** Define it at the organization to grant it across projects.
- **Editor plus a deny list as a homemade custom role.** The list never keeps up with new permissions.
- **A time condition on Owner, Editor or Viewer**, or an expiring binding sitting beside a permanent grant of the same role.
- **Counting generated recommendations as evidence**, or applying all of them without review.

## Putting it together

A defensible baseline: org policies at the organization node (deny external IPs, restrict locations, block service account key creation, disable serial port access); folders per department and environment with group-based IAM; project-level grants only for exceptions; deny policies for protected actions; PAM for elevation; and an aggregated audit sink at the organization.

## Exam tips

- **Hierarchy inheritance:** IAM and Organization Policy flow down; put the baseline at the org node or folder, never rely on per-project configuration.
- **Who versus what:** IAM controls who can act; Organization Policy controls what can be configured, and a project Owner cannot override it without `orgpolicy.policyAdmin`.
- **Roles:** prefer predefined, then custom (300 per org and per project); basic roles are the wrong answer in production.
- **Baseline:** org policies at the org node, group-based IAM on folders, deny policies for protected actions, PAM for elevation.
- **Groups over users:** bind roles to Google Groups at the lowest node that satisfies the need.
- **Deny beats allow:** deny policies are evaluated first, inherit downward, and cannot be overridden lower; PAB can only block, never grant.
- **Separation of duties:** disjoint deployers/approvers groups, and separate policy admins from workload owners; SoD is preventive, auditing is detective.
- **Temporary elevation:** use Privileged Access Manager or service account impersonation with conditions, not permanent powerful roles or downloaded keys.
- **Least-privilege reporting access:** scope the role to the data (for example `roles/billing.viewer`), not to Viewer on everything.
- **Custom role scope:** grantable only within the organization or project that owns it, so define it at the organization for use across many projects; you must add new permissions yourself.
- **Planned window versus on-demand elevation:** a `request.time` condition on predefined roles for a known window; PAM (30 minutes to 7 days, approval, justification) for requested elevation; neither works with Owner, Editor or Viewer.
- **An unconditional binding of the same role defeats any expiry condition.**
- **Evidence:** the IAM recommender uses at most 90 days of usage and applies nothing by itself; Policy Analyzer reports allow-policy grants only, not use and not deny policies.
